full_title: MONICA M. PONTIANO, ROSALYN M. MATANDAG, ELSIE R. BALINGASA, CRISELDA J. ESPINOZA, MIGUEL R. PANGLILINGAN, MARLON A. VILLA, AND LOUIE T. DELA CRUZ, COMPLAINANTS VS. ATTY. FABIAN A. GAPPI, RESPONDENT.
subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
syllabus_topic: IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > A. Legal Ethics (CPRA) > 8. Duties and Responsibilities of Lawyers (CPRA) > e. Competence and Diligence (Canon IV)
topics: Gross negligence: missing every hearing and failing to file the position paper
Disregard of the Labor Arbiter's processes (Canon 11, CPR)
Three-year suspension for gross negligence plus dishonesty (Olvida v. Gonzales)
Separate fine for ignoring IBP-CBD directives
doctrine:
A lawyer who **fails to attend any of the scheduled hearings and fails to file his clients' position paper despite their reminders**, causing the dismissal of their illegal dismissal complaint, is guilty of gross negligence under **Rule 18.03, Canon 18 of the Code of Professional Responsibility (CPR)**. Once a lawyer takes up a client's cause, he must attend to it with competence, diligence, care and devotion, whether he accepts it for a fee or for free; neglect of a legal matter entrusted to him is inexcusable negligence for which he is administratively liable. Deliberately failing to attend hearings ordered by the Labor Arbiter also shows willful disregard of lawful orders, contrary to **Canon 11**.

A lawyer who hands his clients, for signature, a document that would withdraw their complaint while representing that it merely formalizes his withdrawal as counsel commits **dishonesty and deceit in violation of Rule 1.01, Canon 1** of the CPR and of the lawyer's oath to "do no falsehood."

On the penalty, the Court reiterated *Olvida v. Gonzales*: gross negligence in failing to file a position paper, coupled with dishonesty toward the client, warrants **suspension from the practice of law for three years**. A respondent's failure to answer, attend the mandatory conference and file a position paper before the IBP-CBD shows willful disregard of its authority (Canons 11 and 12, CPR) and is separately penalized with a **fine (here P15,000.00)**.
facts:
Complainants were among the 16 complainants in an illegal dismissal case (NLRC NCR Case No. 12-16403-13 and 01-00057-14) before the Labor Arbiter (LA). Respondent Atty. Fabian A. Gappi was their counsel. He did not attend a single scheduled hearing.

Before March 11, 2014, the deadline for their position paper, complainants went to respondent's office to ask about it, and he told them, "Ako na ang bahala." He filed no position paper. On March 11, 2014, complainants returned and asked him to withdraw as their counsel. Respondent prepared a document that supposedly formalized his withdrawal, but on reading it complainants found that it was a withdrawal of their illegal dismissal complaint. They refused to sign it. In a Decision dated April 7, 2014, the LA dismissed the complaint because no position paper had been filed.

Complainants filed an administrative complaint with the IBP. Respondent filed no answer, did not appear at the mandatory conference set on April 6, 2018 (which complainants also missed) or at the reset conference on June 1, 2018, and filed no position paper. The IBP-CBD found him liable under Rule 1.01 of Canon 1, Canon 11, and Rule 18.03 of Canon 18 of the CPR and recommended a two-year suspension. On February 15, 2019, the IBP Board of Governors (IBP-BOG) adopted the findings but increased the suspension to three years and added a P15,000.00 fine for his failure to attend the mandatory conference and file the required pleadings.

In his motion for reconsideration, respondent blamed complainants' indecision over whether to replace him as counsel and the long process of reading and evaluating the evidence of all 16 complainants. The IBP-BOG denied the motion on August 22, 2020.
issues: Whether respondent is administratively liable under Rule 18.03 of Canon 18, Canon 11, and Rule 1.01 of Canon 1 of the CPR for his handling of complainants' illegal dismissal case.
Whether the IBP-BOG's recommended penalty of three years' suspension and a P15,000.00 fine is proper.
ruling:
**1. Yes, respondent is liable.** The Court adopted the findings of the IBP-CBD as modified by the IBP-BOG. Respondent failed to appear at any scheduled hearing, failed to file the position paper despite his own clients' reminders, and tried to deceive them with a document that would have withdrawn their complaint. The complaint was dismissed to their prejudice. Respondent never repudiated these facts and "even implicitly admitted them" through the explanations in his motion for reconsideration.

These facts showed gross negligence and gross inefficiency, a "propensity to disobey lawful processes of the LA," and dishonesty. Adopting the IBP-CBD's discussion: under Canon 18 and Rule 18.03, a lawyer must serve his client with competence and diligence, for a fee or for free, and neglect of an entrusted legal matter is inexcusable negligence; deliberately failing to attend hearings ordered by the LA shows willful disregard of orders, contrary to Canon 11; and deliberately misrepresenting the document he gave his clients to sign violated Rule 1.01 of Canon 1 and his oath, revealing "basic moral flaws that make him unfit to practice law."

**2. Yes, the penalty is proper.** In *Olvida v. Gonzales*, the Court imposed a three-year suspension on a lawyer who was grossly negligent (he failed to file a position paper) and dishonest with his client (he concealed the resulting adverse decision), even raising the IBP's four-month recommendation despite the absence of a motion for reconsideration. Like the lawyer in *Olvida*, respondent was grossly negligent and dishonest, so the three-year suspension was applied. The Court also adopted the P15,000.00 fine: respondent's failure to attend the mandatory conference and file the required pleadings reflected "willful disregard of the IBP-CBD's authority and disrespect of the board's proceedings," which are clear infractions of Canons 11 and 12 of the CPR.
disposition: Respondent Atty. Fabian A. Gappi was found GUILTY of violating Rule 1.01 of Canon 1, Canon 11, and Rule 18.03 of Canon 18 of the CPR and SUSPENDED from the practice of law for three years, effective upon receipt of the Decision, with a WARNING that a repetition would be dealt with more severely. He was also ORDERED to pay a fine of P15,000.00 for failing to comply with the directives of the IBP-CBD. Copies of the Decision were ordered entered in his personal record and furnished to the Office of the Bar Confidant, the IBP, and the Office of the Court Administrator for circulation to all courts.

bar_questions.q: Atty. Lara represented ten workers in an illegal dismissal case before the Labor Arbiter. She did not appear at any of the scheduled hearings. A week before the deadline for the position paper, the workers asked her about it, and she assured them she would take care of it. She filed nothing, and the Labor Arbiter dismissed the complaint for failure to file a position paper. The workers filed a disbarment complaint. Atty. Lara argues that a lawyer cannot be disciplined for a lapse in handling a case because the clients' remedy is to sue her for damages. Is Atty. Lara administratively liable?

alac.answer: Yes. Atty. Lara is administratively liable for gross negligence in handling her clients' case.
alac.legal_basis: Under Canon 18 and Rule 18.03 of the Code of Professional Responsibility, a lawyer shall serve the client with competence and diligence and shall not neglect a legal matter entrusted to him, and his negligence in connection therewith renders him liable. Once a lawyer takes up a client's cause, she must attend to it with diligence, care and devotion, and neglect of an entrusted legal matter is inexcusable negligence for which she is administratively liable. A lawyer who missed every hearing and failed to file the position paper despite his clients' reminders, causing the dismissal of their illegal dismissal complaint, was held grossly negligent (Pontiano v. Atty. Gappi, A.C. No. 13118, June 28, 2022). The duty now appears under Canon IV (Competence and Diligence) of the CPRA.
alac.application: Atty. Lara missed every hearing and let the deadline for the position paper pass even after her clients specifically asked about it and she assured them she would handle it. Her inaction directly caused the dismissal of the complaint, to her clients' prejudice. This is not a mere lapse but the neglect of an entrusted legal matter, which the Code makes a ground for discipline regardless of any civil action the clients may bring against her.
alac.conclusion: Atty. Lara is administratively liable for gross negligence and may be suspended from the practice of law.

bar_questions.q: Atty. Bert agreed, without charging a fee, to represent a group of farm workers in a labor case. When the workers could not decide whether to keep him or hire another lawyer, Atty. Bert stopped attending hearings and did not file their position paper. He later explained that he was waiting for them to decide and that the evidence of all the workers took long to evaluate. When the workers asked him to withdraw as their counsel, he handed them a paper that he said would formalize his withdrawal; it was in fact a withdrawal of their complaint. The workers noticed and refused to sign. (a) Do the facts that he worked for free and that his clients were undecided excuse his failure to act? (b) What is his liability for the paper he asked them to sign?

alac.answer: (a) No. Neither the absence of a fee nor the clients' indecision excuses his neglect. (b) He is liable for dishonesty and deceit under Rule 1.01, Canon 1 of the CPR, which, together with his gross negligence, warrants a suspension (three years in the controlling case).
alac.legal_basis: A lawyer who takes up a client's cause must serve it with competence and diligence, attending to it with diligence, care and devotion "whether he accepts it for a fee or for free" (Canon 18 and Rule 18.03, CPR). Rule 1.01, Canon 1 forbids dishonest and deceitful conduct, and the lawyer's oath binds him to "do no falsehood." In Pontiano v. Atty. Gappi (A.C. No. 13118, June 28, 2022), the Court held liable a lawyer who offered the same excuses (his clients' indecision about replacing him and the long evaluation of the evidence of 16 complainants) and who presented a withdrawal of the clients' complaint as a mere withdrawal of counsel. Following Olvida v. Gonzales, it suspended him for three years.
alac.application: (a) Atty. Bert's duty of diligence attached when he accepted the case, fee or no fee. While he remained their counsel, the workers' indecision did not suspend his duty to attend hearings and meet deadlines; in Pontiano the same excuses did not prevent a finding of gross negligence. (b) Passing off a withdrawal of the complaint as a withdrawal of counsel is deceit practiced on clients who trusted him. Had they signed, they would have lost their case. This is dishonesty under Rule 1.01, on top of his gross negligence.
alac.conclusion: Atty. Bert is liable for both gross negligence and dishonesty, warranting suspension from the practice of law.

bar_questions.q: In disciplinary proceedings before the IBP Commission on Bar Discipline, Atty. Carlo filed no answer, did not appear at two mandatory conferences, and filed no position paper. The Investigating Commissioner found that he had neglected his client's case and lied to the client about its status, and recommended a two-year suspension. The IBP Board of Governors increased the suspension to three years and added a P15,000.00 fine for his non-compliance with the IBP-CBD's directives. Before the Supreme Court, Atty. Carlo argues that (a) his non-participation in the IBP proceedings cannot be separately penalized because it is not the act complained of, and (b) the penalty cannot be raised above the Investigating Commissioner's recommendation. Rule on his arguments.

alac.answer: Both arguments fail. (a) His disregard of the IBP-CBD's directives may be separately penalized with a fine. (b) The Supreme Court determines the penalty on the facts and may adopt the IBP Board's heavier penalty.
alac.legal_basis: In Pontiano v. Atty. Gappi (A.C. No. 13118, June 28, 2022), the Court adopted the IBP Board of Governors' modification that raised the suspension from two to three years and added a P15,000.00 fine. It held that the respondent's failure to attend the mandatory conference and file the required pleadings reflected "willful disregard of the IBP-CBD's authority and disrespect of the board's proceedings," which are clear infractions of Canons 11 and 12 of the CPR. Quoting Olvida v. Gonzales, the Court explained that it exercises its discretion on the penalty on the basis of the facts of the case, and in Olvida it imposed a three-year suspension in place of the IBP's four-month recommendation.
alac.application: (a) Atty. Carlo's failure to answer, attend the mandatory conferences, and file a position paper is a distinct infraction against the disciplinary process, separate from the neglect and dishonesty charged. A separate fine is proper. (b) The IBP's recommendation does not bind the Supreme Court, which fixes the penalty based on the facts. Since Atty. Carlo was both grossly negligent and dishonest toward his client, a three-year suspension is consistent with the penalty imposed in Pontiano and Olvida.
alac.conclusion: The Court may suspend Atty. Carlo for three years and fine him P15,000.00 for ignoring the IBP-CBD's directives.

notes: The decision applied the 1988 Code of Professional Responsibility. It predates the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (A.M. No. 22-09-01-SC, dated April 11, 2023 per the Court's citation in A.C. No. 11889), on which the 2027 syllabus is based. The CPRA cross-reference in the suggested answers (Canon IV, Competence and Diligence) points to the syllabus heading and is not part of the ruling. One quoted IBP passage cites "Rule 18.03 of Canon 8"; this is a typographical error for Canon 18.
